report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Organ scores can conceal recent instability.
We studied confirmed six-hour deterioration in six organs with low recorded severity among 19,690 adults with sepsis in MIMIC-IV, eICU, CareVue and SICdb.
Using a 175-variable model reduced from 552, we compared 3,072 combinations of 12 historical sources.

With hourly predictions, at least four hours between alerts and 0.50 alerts per patient, the model using ten sources captured 319 eICU events versus 245 using current information alone (+30.2%; difference 74, 95% CI 49-106.5).
Gains were 34.6% in CareVue (144 versus 107) and 81.5% in SICdb (49 versus 27); using six sources captured 312 eICU events.
Training with incomplete records increased capture from 180 to 211 (+31) under 50% withholding.
Retrieving one existing laboratory record improved timely correct organ selection from 145 to 159 (+9.7%).
Repeated new low-severity measurements changed earlier history's value.
Models were evaluated without retraining in 1,661 adults with pancreatitis-related conditions.
Identical organ scores can conceal different clinical courses. 1, 2 An organ that has recently improved after dysfunction may carry a different risk from one that has remained stable.
text.formatted: Identical organ scores can conceal different clinical courses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">2</ref> An organ that has recently improved after dysfunction may carry a different risk from one that has remained stable.

text.text: Current scores omit how long the abnormality lasted, the support required during recovery and the sequence of improvement.

Recovery after acute kidney injury illustrates how apparent normalisation can coexist with continuing vulnerability to recurrent injury. 3 We asked whether these earlier changes help identify which of six organs currently recorded at low severity is most likely to deteriorate over the next six hours.

text.text: Models using physiological time series can anticipate circulatory failure and cardiorespiratory instability. 4, 5 A systematic review has examined the predictive value of repeated measurements in critical care. 6 Studies of organ trajectories also describe sepsis subphenotypes and predict deterioration. 7, 8 The remaining question is how much earlier history adds once current physiology, treatment and measurement timing are known and the organ is recorded at low severity.

text.text: Clinical usefulness also depends on which organ is selected for reassessment, when an alert is issued and how repeat alerts are suppressed within the available workload. 9 Electronic health records contain detailed histories, but reviewing an entire ICU stay at every assessment is impractical.

text.text: Differences in charting systems also make large sets of derived variables difficult to transfer between hospitals.
A useful summary should improve prediction beyond current clinical information while requiring few additional record sources.

The number of model variables alone does not describe this requirement: a derived organ state may rely on laboratory tests, ventilator settings and infusion records. 10, 11 We evaluated how much of the benefit of organ history could be retained using fewer record sources (Fig. 1).

text.text: We compared all 3,072 distinct combinations, including a derived organ state only when the records needed to calculate it were available.
We tested history beyond current physiology and measurement patterns and compared compact history from ten sources and brief history from six sources with the full 175-variable model.
We then evaluated hourly organ reassessment, incomplete records, retrieval of existing laboratory results and changes in the value of earlier history as new measurements arrived.

We studied 19,690 adults with sepsis across four databases: 12,905 in MIMIC-IV (8,990 fitting, 1,955 auxiliary development/calibration, and 1,960 held-out evaluation patients), 4,983 across 114 hospitals in eICU-CRD, 1,288 in MIMIC-III CareVue, and 514 in the European SICdb cohort (Fig. 1; Table 1; Supplementary Tables 1 2).

text.text: At each assessment, we predicted confirmed deterioration (SOFA component >=2 sustained across three consecutive hourly positions) within six hours-with 12-and 24-hour extensions-in each of the six organ systems (respiratory, coagulation, hepatic, circulatory, central nervous, and renal) currently recorded below threshold (Fig. 1).

text.text: MIMIC-IV supplied model training and internal evaluation, eICU supported selection using both databases, CareVue tested temporal shift across an earlier charting era, and SICdb provided held-out external validation.
Low current severity did not erase risk associated with prior organ involvement.

Standardising for the active index organ and entry route, six-hour circulatory deterioration risk in MIMIC-IV was 15.69% with prior circulatory involvement versus 1.07% without it (6.33% versus 0.89% in eICU), and respiratory risk was 18.24% versus 7.44% in MIMIC-IV (11.55% versus 3.26% in eICU; Supplementary Fig. 1a; Supplementary Table 4).

text.text: Excess risk also persisted in coagulation (8.49% versus 1.11% in MIMIC-IV; 6.08% versus 0.57% in eICU), renal (10.05% versus 1.09%; 3.40% versus 0.58%), and neurological systems (5.01% versus 1.55%; 7.44% versus 2.77%).

Conditioning on each patient's eligible organ set and total number of organs that deteriorated within the prediction horizon at each assessment confirmed that prior history localised which organ would deteriorate within the same patient, reducing conditional log loss by 0.1396 in MIMIC-IV (95% confidence interval 0.1231-0.1547) and 0.1093 in eICU (0.0654-0.1554; Supplementary Fig. 1b; Supplementary Table 5).

text.text: The compact history (163 columns) achieved AUROCs of 0.9114 and 0.8695, log losses of 0.07927 and 0.05173, and lifted eICU within-patient organ discrimination from 0.8421 to 0.8770.

Scheduled six-hour capture (0.50 alerts/patient) increased from 363 to 382 in MIMIC-IV, 219 to 272 in eICU (282 with full history), 108 to 126 in CareVue, and 26 to 46 in SICdb (Table 2; Supplementary Table 39).

text.text: Consistent gains held at 12 and 24 hours, with eICU median onset lead times of 2 hours (interquartile range 1-3) at 6 hours, 5 hours (2-7) at 12 hours, and 7 hours (3-14) at 24 hours (Supplementary Fig. 3a,b,d; Supplementary Tables 6 and 37).

text.text: Historical gains persisted in three comparisons addressing current information and measurement frequency.

First, expanding the current baseline from 67 to 91 variables yielded 205 eICU captures (log loss 0.05427), whereas adding compact history on top of the 91-variable baseline reduced log loss to 0.05265 and increased capture to 270 (274 with full history; Supplementary Tables 6 7).

text.text: Second, restricting the index assessment to observations with a target-organ measurement within the preceding three hours preserved historical gains in MIMIC-IV (AUROC 0.8742 to 0.8950) and eICU (0.7936 to 0.8405; Supplementary Table 8).

text.text: Third, decomposing the model with 175 variables in eICU showed that current values/states captured 238 events (log loss 0.05450), adding recording-process indicators captured 219 (0.05406), adding 90 numerical-history variables captured 240 (0.05378), and adding the 18 derived organ-state history variables lifted capture to 282 (0.05203; Supplementary Fig. 3c; Supplementary Table 31), surpassing simple summary statistics plus state durations (256 captures; Supplementary Fig. 2d; Supplementary Table 11).
